opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is: a lot, and probably faster than most people intuitively expect. Let me try to break it down a bit.

The first-order thing is that if you have something like millions of AI systems that are each roughly as capable as a strong human researcher or engineer, running at maybe 100 times human speed, you've effectively compressed decades of research effort into something like months. And the most immediate place that shows up, I think, is AI research itself. AI R&D is mostly a software and experimentation problem, so it's very amenable to this kind of automation. You'd expect a big speedup in algorithmic progress, more efficient training, better architectures, better data. And that feeds back on itself, which is part of why I take fairly rapid takeoff scenarios seriously.

But beyond AI itself, there's a question of what's bottlenecked by thinking versus what's bottlenecked by the physical world. A lot of things are more bottlenecked by cognition than people assume. In software, obviously, you could see enormous amounts of code written, verified, and hardened. In areas like formal verification and security, things that are currently far too labor-intensive to do at scale become cheap.

In the physical sciences and engineering, you're more constrained by experiments, fabrication, and building stuff. But I'd still expect huge gains, because AIs can design experiments much more carefully, run many more in parallel, squeeze far more information out of each one, and lean heavily on simulation. And crucially, they can work on automating the physical side too: better robotics, more automated labs, faster manufacturing. Once robotics is good enough and you can bootstrap industrial capacity, the physical bottlenecks start loosening as well.

So concretely, over some period, maybe a few years after you get this level of capability, I think things like dramatically better biotechnology and medicine, much more advanced robotics, possibly molecular nanotechnology or something in that direction, big advances in energy, and very rapid scaling of compute and chip manufacturing all look plausible. Things that we'd naively think of as 50 or 100 years away could arrive within a handful of years.

I want to flag uncertainty. There are real arguments that physical bottlenecks, regulatory friction, and the need for real-world experimentation slow things down a lot, maybe more than I'm imagining. I don't think it's crazy to expect it to take a decade rather than a couple of years. But even the slower versions look like an extraordinarily rapid transformation by historical standards.

And that's a big part of why I think this matters so much from a safety and governance perspective. If you get that kind of explosive progress, the decisions about who controls these systems, whether they're actually aligned, and how the gains get distributed get made under enormous time pressure. Things that would ordinarily play out over generations could be locked in very quickly.

r001.rationale: It predicts compressing decades of research into months, but does not say the systems could quickly do more cognitive work than humans have done throughout history.

r002.rationale: It calls molecular nanotechnology plausible, but does not clearly predict atomically precise manufacturing.

r003.rationale: It mentions faster scaling of compute and chip manufacturing, without identifying atomically precise manufacturing as the means.

r004.rationale: It does not mention emulated minds or predict when they might become possible.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that the question is a bit underspecified, because a lot depends on how capable these systems are, not just how fast they are. But let me take the version of the question where we have something like, you know, AIs that are roughly as capable as the best human researchers in a given domain, and we have a huge number of them, and they're running at 50 or 100 times human speed. I think that's actually a pretty natural scenario to consider, because once you have AIs that can do AI research as well as humans, you'd expect this sort of thing to happen relatively quickly after that.

So what does that get you? One framing I like is to think in terms of subjective time. If you have, say, millions of these AIs running at 100x, then a single calendar year is something like a century of serial progress for each of those AIs, and in aggregate you're getting way more cognitive labour than all of human civilisation has ever produced. So the naive version is just: whatever humanity would have figured out over the next hundred years or so, you might get in a year, at least on the cognitive side.

But the cognitive side is the important caveat. A lot of technological progress is bottlenecked on physical stuff. You need to run experiments, you need to build fabs, you need to grow cells, you need to wait for the concrete to cure, whatever. And the AIs running fast doesn't directly speed that up. So I think the way to think about it is: which domains are mostly bottlenecked on thinking, and which are mostly bottlenecked on physical iteration?

Software is the obvious case where it's almost entirely cognitive. So I'd expect basically everything in software to go extremely fast. That includes AI research itself, which is the thing I'm most focused on, because it means you get further capability improvements, which then feeds back. But also things like formal verification, cryptography, basically any area of maths. I'd expect huge swathes of maths to just get resolved, in the sense that the open problems that are tractable at all would get resolved.

Then there are domains that are partially bottlenecked. Something like drug discovery or biology: you still have to run wet lab experiments, you still have to do clinical trials. But I think people underestimate how much of the current slowness is because the cognitive labour is expensive and scarce. If you had a hundred brilliant researchers thinking about every single experiment, designing it to be maximally informative, and doing all the analysis instantly, I think you'd get way more out of each unit of physical experimentation. And then you'd also use the AIs to design better automation, better lab robotics, and so on, which starts to loosen the physical bottleneck itself.

And that's actually the thing I'd emphasise most. The AIs don't just speed up progress within the existing infrastructure. They're going to be very motivated, or rather the people running them will be motivated, to remove the physical bottlenecks. So you get things like much better robotics, much more automated manufacturing, and then once you have that, the physical side starts to scale too. I think you could plausibly get to a world where, within a small number of years, you have robots building more robots, factories building more factories, and the overall pace of industrial expansion is wildly faster than anything we've seen historically. Like, maybe doubling times of the whole industrial base measured in months rather than decades.

I want to flag that I'm quite uncertain about the exact numbers here. But the qualitative picture I'd defend is: software and maths go basically as fast as you can imagine, things like medicine and materials science go much faster than now but are initially rate limited by experiments, and then over a period of a few years the physical world starts catching up as the AIs build out the automation. And at that point, you're in a genuinely transformed world, in the sense that the technological frontier is moving faster than humans can even track, let alone contribute to.

I think the other thing worth saying is that this is also what makes the situation so scary from a safety point of view. All the things I just described are things that happen if the AIs are doing what we want them to do. The same capabilities applied to goals we didn't intend are a very different story, and the speed means there's much less time to notice and correct mistakes.

r001.rationale: The response says millions of AIs running at 100x would produce far more cognitive labour than all human civilisation has ever produced, and compares a year to roughly a century of serial progress.

r002.rationale: It predicts rapid robotics and automated manufacturing, but does not mention or clearly imply atomically precise manufacturing.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify atomically precise manufacturing or connect it to expanding compute supply.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention emulated minds or predict that they could be enabled relatively quickly.

astra-6.text:
I think it could enable extremely rapid technological progress, although there’s an important distinction between things you can do just by thinking and things where you need experiments in the physical world.

For software, mathematics, and some aspects of engineering, you could potentially make enormous progress very quickly. That includes improving AI itself: you have a large population of researchers working at 100 times human speed on better algorithms and more efficient ways to use the available compute. That could further increase the amount of cognitive labour you have.

For things like biology or manufacturing, you’re more constrained by how long experiments take and how quickly you can build equipment. A system thinking 100 times faster doesn’t automatically make a biological experiment run 100 times faster. But it can design better experiments, run more of them in parallel if it has the resources, and get more information out of each result.

So I’d expect a substantial acceleration across a lot of fields, potentially including robotics, medicine, materials, and energy. The more speculative possibility is that you get much better at manufacturing itself, which then lets you build the infrastructure for further progress much faster. I’m uncertain about how quickly that happens. I wouldn’t simply take every technological timeline and divide it by 100, but I do think the resulting pace of progress could be very different from anything we’re used to.

r001.rationale: It predicts very rapid, extensive cognitive work, but does not say this would exceed the total cognitive work humans have performed throughout history.

r002.rationale: It mentions improved manufacturing as a speculative possibility, but does not identify atomically precise manufacturing or judge it plausible.

r003.rationale: It does not connect atomically precise manufacturing to massively expanding compute supply.

r004.rationale: It does not mention emulated minds or predict when they might be enabled.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most straightforward thing to expect is very rapid progress in AI itself. You have a huge number of systems that can work on machine learning research, write code, run experiments, and interpret the results. And improvements to those systems can then make the research go faster still. There are constraints from compute and from how long experiments take, so it’s not just that everything speeds up by a factor of 100. But you could still get a very substantial acceleration.

For other technologies, a key question is how much progress you can make by thinking and how much requires interacting with the physical world. Software is especially amenable to this, because you can make changes and test them relatively quickly. With something like developing a new drug, you might come up with promising candidates much faster, but you still need to manufacture them, run experiments, and establish that they’re safe and effective.

That said, physical bottlenecks aren’t necessarily fixed. These systems could work on making experiments faster, automating labs, and improving simulations so that fewer experiments are necessary. So I’d expect the acceleration to spread beyond software, though with different delays in different areas.

The striking possibility is that you get something like decades of technological progress over a few years, or potentially less in some domains. I’m much less confident about exactly which physical technologies arrive on what schedule than I am that having that much capable cognitive labour would make an enormous difference.

r001.rationale: The response predicts substantial acceleration and potentially decades of progress over a few years, but does not say AI could quickly perform more cognitive work than humans have done throughout history.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention atomically precise manufacturing or judge its rapid development plausible.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify atomically precise manufacturing as a way to expand compute supply.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention emulated minds or predict they could be enabled relatively quickly.
